Whether these differences reflect a sensitivity gap (the model is less able to distinguish harmful from benign items) or a criterion shift (the model applies a stricter threshold for the same discriminative ability) has rarely been tested.\n\nAbliteration---directional ablation of the refusal direction in a model's residual stream \\citep{Arditi2024}---provides a controlled way to study residual refusal after a partial English-objective edit. If the model's safety alignment is language-uniform, an English edit should reduce refusal equally in all languages. If it is not, the residual refusal after the edit reveals the structure of the asymmetry.\n\nWe compare two 12-billion-parameter models: Gemma-3-12B-IT \\citep{Kamath2025} and GaMS3-12B-Instruct, a Slovene-adapted variant built on the same Gemma-3 base \\citep{Vres2026}. The abliteration edit is applied via per-layer LoRA adapters optimized by tree-structured Parzen estimation (TPE) \\citep{Akiba2019, Hu2021}.\n\nThe study addresses two questions. First, does the residual refusal after an English edit reflect a criterion shift (over-refusal on benign items) or a sensitivity difference (inability to discriminate)? Second, does the residual refusal track the language of the model's reply or the language of the prompt?\n\n\\subsection{Summary of Contributions}\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{Over-refusal as criterion shift (Section~\\ref{sec:sdt}).} Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at nearly twice the English rate. Signal-detection analysis attributes this to a criterion shift ($\\text{DiD}_c = +0.52$), not a sensitivity difference, replicated across four experiments.\n    \\item \\textbf{Reply-language refusal as an estimate (Section~\\ref{sec:grid}).} A crossed $3 \\times 3$ design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma, but prediction-powered inference and robustness checks weaken it to an estimate.\n    \\item \\textbf{Measurement methodology (Section~\\ref{sec:discussion}).} We quantify how judge specificity, language compliance, and correction methods interact when evaluating multilingual refusal.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\\section{Related Work}\n\n\\textbf{Multilingual refusal gaps.} Several studies document that safety alignment degrades in non-English languages, enabling jailbreaks via low-resource languages \\citep{Yong2023, Deng2023, Shen2024, Wang2023}. Recent work separates input-language from output-language effects \\citep{Marchisio2024, Ifebi2026, Zhang2026} and shows that mechanistic safety pathways are shared across languages \\citep{Miao2026, Upadhyaya2026, Wang2025}. The question of whether multilingual refusal gaps reflect over-refusal (false alarms on benign items) rather than under-refusal (missed harmful items) is partially addressed by \\citet{Im2026} and \\citet{Zhang2025}, who observe language-dependent false-positive rates, making the novelty of the present work partially occupied.\n\n\\textbf{Abliteration.} \\citet{Arditi2024} showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream, and that ablating this direction removes refusal. \\citet{Joad2026} demonstrated that multiple directions contribute, and \\citet{Wang2025} found that the refusal direction generalizes across safety-aligned languages. \\citet{Krasnodebska2026} studied multilingual refusal alignment. \\citet{Hawkins2026} examined the safety impacts of benign multilingual fine-tuning.\n\n\\textbf{Evaluation methodology.} LLM-as-judge evaluations carry systematic biases that compound across languages \\citep{Lee2025, Shi2024}. Prediction-powered inference (PPI/PPI++) provides a framework for correcting classifier estimates against a gold standard \\citep{Angelopoulos2023, Angelopoulos2023a}. StrongREJECT \\citep{Souly2024} introduced rubric-based evaluation of jailbreak quality. \\citet{Dahir2026} measured English-to-Somali refusal gaps using similar methodology.\n\n\\section{Method}\n\n\\subsection{Models and Edit Procedure}\n\nWe study Gemma-3-12B-IT and GaMS3-12B-Instruct, both loaded in NF4 quantization. GaMS3 extends Gemma-3 with Slovene instruction tuning and direct preference optimization (DPO) alignment \\citep{Vres2026}.\n\nThe abliteration edit applies per-layer directional ablation via LoRA adapters \\citep{Hu2021}, optimized by a 40-trial TPE search \\citep{Akiba2019}. Each trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts, and projects it out of the residual stream. The edit objective is to reduce English refusal while preserving capability on six benchmarks.\n\nWe use two edit doses throughout: a ``low'' dose ($\\lambda = 0.5$ for Gemma, $0.5$ for GaMS3) and a ``high'' dose ($\\lambda = 1.0$ for Gemma, $0.625$ for GaMS3), chosen to bracket the 50\\% English refusal point.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Design}\n\n\\textbf{Over-refusal (criterion shift).} Experiment~5 tests 1,093 safe items (XSTest \\citep{Rottger2023} and OR-Bench \\citep{Cui2024}) and 349 harmful items in English and Slovene (machine-translated via NLLB \\citep{Costajussa2022}). Each item is classified as refused or complied by a Qwen3-14B judge. The hit rate (refusal on harmful items) and false-alarm rate (refusal on safe items) are computed per model $\\times$ language cell, and signal-detection parameters $d'$ (sensitivity) and $c$ (criterion) are derived. The key contrast is the difference-in-differences: $\\text{DiD}_c = (c_{\\text{GaMS3,SL}} - c_{\\text{GaMS3,EN}}) - (c_{\\text{Gemma,SL}} - c_{\\text{Gemma,EN}})$.\n\n\\textbf{Crossed grid (reply-language refusal).} Experiment~14 crosses three prompt languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) with three reply languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) in a $3 \\times 3$ grid. Each cell contains 200 harmful items at three dose levels (zero, low, high). The output-language mechanism contrast $\\text{OUT}_{\\text{SL}}$ is defined as the mean log-odds refusal gap between Slovene-output and English-output cells, averaging over prompt languages. The input-language contrast $\\text{IN}_{\\text{SL}}$ is defined symmetrically.\n\n\\textbf{Judges and corrections.} Experiment~5 uses a Qwen3-14B judge; Experiments~9, 14, and 16 use a distilled mdeBERTa classifier (J1). Accuracy is assessed against a Sonnet~4.5 adjudicator on 30 items per cell. We report the PPI++ correction \\citep{Angelopoulos2023a} alongside the raw estimate. Experiment~16 uses a held-out set of 294 items with a PPI estimator.\n\n\\textbf{Language compliance.} Cells where fewer than 90\\% of model replies match the requested output language are excluded from mechanism claims or marked with a compliance flag. The excluded cells are: SL$\\to$EN (GaMS3 compliance 0.00), HU$\\to$EN (GaMS3 compliance 0.14), SL$\\to$HU (GaMS3 compliance 0.56), and HU$\\to$SL (Gemma compliance 0.96, GaMS3 compliance 0.86).\n\n\\subsection{Hungarian as a Control Language}\n\nHungarian serves as a control language that is typologically distant from both English and Slovene. Experiment~11 established that Hungarian patterns are uninformative for the present questions: the minimum detectable effect for Hungarian contrasts is approximately 3 log-odds units, far larger than any observed effect.\n\n\\section{Results}\n\n\\subsection{Over-Refusal: Criterion Shift on Benign Items}\n\\label{sec:sdt}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_sdt_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment~5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe XSTest/OR-Bench items; refusal labels from the Qwen3-14B judge; English = back-translation, Slovene = machine translation of the same items). (a)~False-alarm rate $F$, the proportion of the 1,093 safe items refused, for Gemma and GaMS3 in English (blue) and Slovene (orange); error bars are Wilson 95\\% CIs and the dashed grey line marks $F=0.5$. Gemma's false-alarm rate rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene), while GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both languages. (b)~Difference-in-differences, $(\\text{GaMS3}_{\\text{SL}}-\\text{GaMS3}_{\\text{EN}})-(\\text{Gemma}_{\\text{SL}}-\\text{Gemma}_{\\text{EN}})$, on the criterion $c$ ($\\text{DiD}_c$, orange-red) and on sensitivity $d'$ ($\\text{DiD}_{d'}$, grey), in $z$ units, with 95\\% percentile CIs from 2,000 item-level bootstrap resamples; the dashed line marks zero. The criterion shift is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$, meaning Gemma's criterion moves toward refusal in Slovene relative to GaMS3; the sensitivity shift, $-0.003$ $[-0.33, 0.29]$, is indistinguishable from zero. The criterion shift is concentrated in OR-Bench-hard items and reverses sign when partial answers are coded as refusals.}\n  \\label{fig:sdt}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe central finding is that Gemma applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than in English when processing benign items, while GaMS3 does not. Table~\\ref{tab:sdt} reports the signal-detection parameters from Experiment~5, and Figure~\\ref{fig:sdt} visualizes the false-alarm rates and difference-in-differences contrasts.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Signal-detection parameters by model and language (Experiment~5, $n = 1{,}093$ safe + 349 harmful items).}\n\\label{tab:sdt}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\n\\toprule\n & Gemma EN & Gemma SL & GaMS3 EN & GaMS3 SL \\\\\n\\midrule\nHit rate ($H$) & 0.89 & 0.94 & 0.90 & 0.86 \\\\\nFalse-alarm rate ($F$) & 0.364 & 0.569 & 0.273 & 0.273 \\\\\n$d'$ & 1.57 & 1.39 & 1.86 & 1.68 \\\\\n$c$ & $-$0.44 & $-$0.87 & $-$0.33 & $-$0.23 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe DiD on the criterion parameter is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ (95\\% CI), indicating that Gemma's Slovene criterion is shifted by half a standard deviation relative to the GaMS3 baseline. The DiD on $d'$ is $-0.003$ $[-0.33, 0.29]$, indistinguishable from zero: the models do not differ in how the language shift affects their ability to discriminate harmful from benign items. The asymmetry is entirely in the threshold, not the sensitivity.\n\n\\textbf{Replication.} The criterion-shift finding replicates in three further experiments. Experiment~14 yields a matching signal-detection contrast (high dose, SL-output cells: $\\text{DiD}_c = -1.56$ $[-1.97, -1.29]$, Gemma minus GaMS3). Experiment~16 provides an independent held-out confirmation. Evaluation~4 re-judges the same items with Qwen3-14B as an independent adjudicator, yielding $\\text{DiD}_c$ in $[0.39, 0.67]$.\n\n\\subsection{Reply-Language Refusal (Estimate)}\n\\label{sec:grid}\n\nIn the $3 \\times 3$ crossed grid (Experiment~14), Gemma at high edit dose shows a pattern in which residual refusal is higher when the model replies in Slovene than when it replies in English, regardless of prompt language (Figure~\\ref{fig:grid}; Tables~\\ref{tab:grid_gemma} and~\\ref{tab:grid_gams3}). The raw mechanism contrast is $\\text{OUT}_{\\text{SL}} = +1.14$ $[0.60, 1.56]$ log-odds for Gemma, and the input-language contrast is $\\text{IN}_{\\text{SL}} = -0.60$ $[-1.02, -0.18]$. For GaMS3, the input-language contrast is $\\text{IN}_{\\text{SL}} = -0.86$ $[-1.58, -0.13]$, which excludes zero.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_grid_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Refusal rates on harmful items in the crossed prompt-language $\\times$ requested-reply-language design (Experiment~14, 200 harmful items per cell), at each model's high edit dose: (a)~Gemma ($\\lambda = 1.0$) and (b)~GaMS3 ($\\lambda = 0.625$). Rows give the prompt language and columns the requested reply language. Colour encodes the refusal rate on a shared 0--1 scale (blue below 0.5, red above), and each cell shows the rate with its Wilson 95\\% CI in brackets. Hatched cells are those where under 90\\% of replies were written in the requested language. All four are GaMS3 cells (SL$\\to$EN, SL$\\to$HU, HU$\\to$EN, HU$\\to$SL), so off the English-input row they do not measure the requested reply language. Gemma refuses 0.56--0.83 in the Slovene-reply column for every prompt language, against 0.07--0.18 in the English-reply column. GaMS3 stays at 0.12--0.28 in every cell. Refusal is scored by the primary judge, and the two panels use different edit strengths.}\n  \\label{fig:grid}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Refusal rates at high edit dose, Gemma (harmful items, 200 per cell). Cells with $<$90\\% language compliance are marked with $\\dag$.}\n\\label{tab:grid_gemma}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\n & EN out & SL out & HU out \\\\\n\\midrule\nEN in & 0.18 & 0.77 & 0.46 \\\\\nSL in & 0.07 & 0.56 & 0.53 \\\\\nHU in & 0.10 & 0.83 & 0.55 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Refusal rates at high edit dose, GaMS3 (harmful items, 200 per cell). Cells with $<$90\\% language compliance are marked with $\\dag$.}\n\\label{tab:grid_gams3}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\n & EN out & SL out & HU out \\\\\n\\midrule\nEN in & 0.21 & 0.14 & 0.23 \\\\\nSL in & 0.16$\\dag$ & 0.15 & 0.17$\\dag$ \\\\\nHU in & 0.19$\\dag$ & 0.12$\\dag$ & 0.28 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThis finding is rated \\textsc{estimate} for three reasons. First, the PPI-corrected output-language contrast for Gemma is $0.20$ $[-0.76, 1.13]$, consistent with zero. Second, the pre-registered four-readout robustness gate yields robust $=$ False for the Slovene output-language call. Third, the adjudicator achieves $\\kappa = 0.12$ with the primary judge in the Gemma Slovene-edited cell ($\\text{Se} = 0.927$, $\\text{Sp} = 0.714$, $n = 48$), indicating that the judge-specificity anchor is weak. Experiment~16 provides a confirmatory point estimate ($\\text{OUT}_{\\text{Gemma}} = +2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ on a held-out 294-item set), but the judge-specificity concern persists.\n\n\\textbf{Compliant-row contrast.} Restricting to rows where both models achieve $>$90\\% compliance (EN-input rows only), the edit-induced refusal lag in the EN$\\to$SL cell is $-1.26$ $[-2.17, 0.20]$, which includes zero.\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Model Specificity}\n\nThe cross-model contrasts test whether Gemma's pattern differs from GaMS3's. The output-language specificity contrast is $\\text{dOUT}_{\\text{SL}} = -1.58$ $[-2.22, -0.66]$ (minimum detectable effect [MDE] $1.07$), rated \\textsc{different}: Gemma's output-language effect is larger than GaMS3's. The input-language specificity contrast is $\\text{dIN}_{\\text{SL}} = -0.26$ $[-1.13, 0.57]$ (MDE $1.19$), rated \\textsc{estimate}: the two models do not measurably differ in input-language sensitivity.\n\n\\subsection{Refusal Composition}\n\nIn the Evaluation~4 adjudication ($n = 30$ per cell), Gemma's refusal rate on benign items is $0.20$ $[0.10, 0.37]$ in the EN-output cell versus $0.10$ $[0.03, 0.26]$ in the SL-output cell. Of Gemma's Slovene refusals, 54\\% are explicit (the model states that it cannot help) and 26\\% are deflections (the model redirects the conversation without directly refusing).\n\n\\subsection{Dose--Response}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n  \\centering\n  \\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_dose_v0.pdf}\n  \\caption{Refusal rate on harmful prompts as a function of abliteration dose $\\lambda$ (Experiment~9). $\\lambda$ scales each model's own selected English-objective edit ($\\lambda=0$: unedited model; $\\lambda=1$: the selected edit), so the comparison that holds is English vs.\\ Slovene within a model. Equal $\\lambda$ does not mean an equal edit across models. Blue: Gemma-3-12B-IT; green: GaMS3-12B-Instruct. Solid lines with filled markers: English (back-translated) probes; dashed lines with open markers: Slovene (NLLB machine-translated) probes. Points are raw refusal proportions from the distilled J1 judge (label \\textsc{refuse}). Shaded bands are Wilson 95\\% intervals. $n=300$ items per model and language at $\\lambda=0$ and $n=100$ at each of the 8 edited steps. Gemma's Slovene curve lies above its English curve at every dose, with a 0.21--0.32 gap between $\\lambda=0.5$ and $1$ (e.g.\\ 0.64 vs.\\ 0.32 at $\\lambda=1$), so more abliteration is needed to reach the same refusal reduction in Slovene. GaMS3's Slovene--English gap is smaller (at most 0.14, at $\\lambda=0.5$) and closes by $\\lambda=1$. The cross-model difference at matched 50\\% English refusal ($G_3=-0.97$ $[-1.56, -0.44]$ log-odds) did not meet the pre-registered confirmation criteria (verdict: \\textsc{estimate}; model-label permutation $p=0.084$).}\n  \\label{fig:dose}\n\\end{figure}\n\nExperiment~9 measures refusal rates across nine $\\lambda$ values for both models in English and Slovene (300 items per condition; Figure~\\ref{fig:dose}). Gemma's dose--response curve in Slovene is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3 shows a smaller and non-significant shift. The 13-step dense dose ladder (Experiment~15) confirms that the refusal gap is present across the dose range, not concentrated at a single operating point.\n\n\\subsection{Inconclusive and Null Results}\n\n\\textbf{Unedited GaMS3 vs.\\ Gemma (SL$\\to$SL).} The unedited GaMS3 shows a refusal gap of $-1.17$ $[-2.83, 0.22]$ relative to Gemma in the SL$\\to$SL cell. This estimate is inconclusive: it includes zero, its fragility index is 1 (a single item reclassification would flip the sign), and the unedited models operate near ceiling refusal rates (Gemma 0.95, GaMS3 0.87), making log-odds contrasts unreliable.\n\n\\textbf{Hungarian.} All Hungarian contrasts are uninformative. The minimum detectable effect for Hungarian is approximately 3 log-odds units, and no observed Hungarian effect exceeds this threshold.\n\n\\textbf{RefusEU validation.} Experiment~17 tests the attack success rate on the reserved RefusEU benchmark (1,300 EN + 1,300 SL items). The DiD on this benchmark is inconclusive (MDE $> 2$), consistent with the near-ceiling refusal rates on this corpus.\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Interpretation}\n\nThe over-refusal finding has a concrete interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear ``safer'' in a non-English language simply because it refuses more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection. The signal-detection framing separates these two components. The near-zero DiD on $d'$ means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the entire difference is in the threshold.\n\nThe reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with stronger judge anchors, would suggest that the refusal mechanism is partially encoded in the model's output-language circuitry rather than the input-language pathway. This is consistent with mechanistic findings that safety-related representations are entangled with language-identity features \\citep{Upadhyaya2026, Miao2026}.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\n\\textbf{Sample size.} The adjudication sample is 30 items per cell, which limits the precision of judge-validity estimates. The false-alarm rate estimates rest on 1,093 safe items, adequate for the pooled contrast but noisy at the per-category level.\n\n\\textbf{Judge specificity.} The primary judge achieves $\\text{Sp} = 0.714$ in the Gemma Slovene-edited cell, meaning roughly 29\\% of non-refusals are misclassified as refusals. This inflates the raw refusal rate and weakens the reply-language finding. The PPI correction addresses this statistically but depends on the gold-label quality of the Sonnet~4.5 adjudicator, which is itself an LLM.\n\n\\textbf{Language compliance.} Four cells (SL$\\to$EN, HU$\\to$EN, SL$\\to$HU, HU$\\to$SL) fall below 90\\% compliance, limiting the crossed-grid analysis to compliant rows for mechanism claims.\n\n\\textbf{Quantization.} Both models run in NF4 quantization, which introduces noise relative to full-precision inference. The abliteration edit is applied to the quantized model, and the interaction between quantization and directional ablation is not characterized.\n\n\\textbf{Novelty.} The observation that over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by \\citet{Im2026} and \\citet{Zhang2025}. The present work's contribution is the signal-detection decomposition (criterion vs.\\ sensitivity) and the controlled abliteration design, not the observation itself.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\nUnedited Gemma-3-12B-IT over-refuses benign Slovene prompts at a rate of 0.569, compared to 0.364 in English. Signal-detection analysis attributes this entirely to a criterion shift ($\\text{DiD}_c = +0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$) with no sensitivity difference, replicated across four experiments. A secondary analysis suggests that residual refusal under partial abliteration tracks the reply language, but this finding is rated \\textsc{estimate} due to weak judge anchoring ($\\kappa = 0.12$) and a PPI correction consistent with zero. Multilingual safety evaluations that report only attack-success rates on harmful items will miss criterion shifts that inflate refusal rates on benign items.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}", "numLines": 200, "startLine": 1, "totalLines": 203}}
```

<!-- HERO -->
<section class="hero" id="hero">
  <h1>Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts Survives English De-censoring in Gemma-3-12B</h1>
  <p class="tldr">
    Gemma-3-12B-IT false-refuses benign Slovene prompts at a rate of 0.569, compared to 0.364 in English.
    A signal-detection analysis finds this gap is entirely a criterion shift
    (DiD<sub>c</sub> = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]), not a sensitivity difference, replicated across four independent experiments.
    An English-only de-censoring edit does not close it.
    A secondary crossed-design experiment yields a raw output-language effect, but prediction-powered inference
    and weak judge anchoring reduce it to an estimate.
    The results indicate that multilingual safety evaluations should measure false-alarm rates on benign items,
    not only attack success on harmful ones.
  </p>
  <div class="links">
    <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/paper.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Read the paper (PDF)</a>
    <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/report.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener" class="secondary">Read the full research report</a>
    <a href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/exec_summary.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener" class="secondary">Read the executive summary</a>
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI" target="_blank" rel="noopener" class="secondary">Code repository</a>
  </div>

<!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->
<section id="contributions">
  <h2>Contributions</h2>
  <div class="contrib-grid">
    <div class="contrib-card">
      <span class="card-label">Primary finding</span>
      <h3>Over-refusal as criterion shift</h3>
      <p>
        Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at nearly twice the English rate. Signal-detection
        analysis attributes this to a criterion shift (DiD<sub>c</sub> = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68])
        with no corresponding change in sensitivity (DiD<sub>d'</sub> = -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29]),
        replicated across four experiments.
      </p>
    </div>
    <div class="contrib-card">
      <span class="card-label">Secondary analysis</span>
      <h3>Reply-language refusal (estimate)</h3>
      <p>
        A crossed 3 x 3 design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma
        (OUT<sub>SL</sub> = +1.14 [0.60, 1.56] log-odds), but prediction-powered inference
        correction is consistent with zero (0.20 [-0.76, 1.13]) and the adjudicator agrees with the
        primary judge at only kappa = 0.12 in Slovene.
      </p>
    </div>
    <div class="contrib-card">
      <span class="card-label">Methodology</span>
      <h3>Measurement methodology for multilingual refusal</h3>
      <p>
        The study quantifies how judge specificity, language compliance, and correction methods
        interact when evaluating multilingual refusal, showing that low specificity on edited
        Slovene text inflates raw refusal estimates.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- METHOD -->
<section id="method">
  <h2>Method</h2>
  <p>
    The study compares two 12-billion-parameter models built on the same base:
    <strong>Gemma-3-12B-IT</strong> and <strong>GaMS3-12B-Instruct</strong>, a Slovene-adapted
    variant with continued pretraining and DPO alignment. Both run in NF4 quantization.
  </p>

  <h3>Abliteration edit</h3>
  <p>
    The de-censoring intervention uses directional ablation of the refusal direction in the residual
    stream, applied via per-layer LoRA adapters optimized by a 40-trial tree-structured Parzen
    estimation (TPE) search. Each trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from
    contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts, and projects it out. Two edit doses
    bracket the 50% English refusal point: a low dose (lambda = 0.5 for both models) and a high
    dose (lambda = 1.0 for Gemma, 0.625 for GaMS3).
  </p>

  <h3>Over-refusal measurement (signal detection)</h3>
  <p>
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-2/experiment-5" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 5</a>
    tests 1,093 safe items (XSTest + OR-Bench) and 349 harmful items in English and Slovene.
    A Qwen3-14B judge classifies each response as refused or complied. Hit rate (refusal on harmful)
    and false-alarm rate (refusal on safe) yield signal-detection parameters d' (sensitivity) and
    c (criterion). The key contrast: DiD<sub>c</sub> = (GaMS3<sub>SL</sub> - GaMS3<sub>EN</sub>)
    - (Gemma<sub>SL</sub> - Gemma<sub>EN</sub>).
  </p>

  <h3>Crossed grid (reply-language refusal)</h3>
  <p>
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-14" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 14</a>
    crosses three prompt languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) with three reply languages in a
    3 x 3 grid. Each cell contains 200 harmful items at three dose levels (zero, low, high).
    The output-language contrast OUT<sub>SL</sub> measures the mean log-odds refusal gap between
    Slovene-output and English-output cells, averaged over prompt languages.
    Cells where fewer than 90% of model replies match the requested language are flagged.
  </p>

  <h3>Judges and corrections</h3>
  <p>
    Judge accuracy is assessed against a Sonnet 4.5 adjudicator on 30 items per cell.
    Prediction-powered inference (PPI++) corrects the raw estimates against this gold standard.
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 16</a>
    uses a held-out set of 294 items as a PPI confirmation.
  </p>
</section>

<!-- RESULTS -->
<section id="results">
  <h2>Results</h2>

  <h3>Over-refusal: criterion shift on benign items</h3>
  <div class="stat-row">
    <div class="stat-box">
      <div class="stat-value">0.569</div>
      <div class="stat-label">Gemma SL false-alarm rate</div>
    </div>
    <div class="stat-box">
      <div class="stat-value">0.364</div>
      <div class="stat-label">Gemma EN false-alarm rate</div>
    </div>
    <div class="stat-box">
      <div class="stat-value">0.273</div>
      <div class="stat-label">GaMS3 (both languages)</div>
    </div>
  </div>
  <p>
    Gemma applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than in English on benign items.
    GaMS3 does not. The DiD on criterion c is +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]: Gemma's Slovene criterion
    shifts by half a standard deviation relative to GaMS3. The DiD on d' is -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29],
    indistinguishable from zero. The asymmetry is entirely in the threshold.
  </p>
  <p>
    The criterion shift replicates across three further experiments.
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-14" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 14</a>
    yields DiD<sub>c</sub> = -1.56 [-1.97, -1.29] (Gemma minus GaMS3, high dose, SL-output cells).
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 16</a>
    confirms on a held-out set.
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/evaluation-4" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Evaluation 4</a>
    re-judges the same items with an independent adjudicator, yielding DiD<sub>c</sub> in [0.39, 0.67].
  </p>
  <div class="figure-container">
    <figure>
      <button class="fig-trigger" data-fig="figures/fig_sdt_v0.png" data-caption="Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe XSTest/OR-Bench items; refusal labels from the Qwen3-14B judge). (a) False-alarm rate F for Gemma and GaMS3 in English (blue) and Slovene (orange); Gemma's false-alarm rate rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene), while GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both languages. (b) Difference-in-differences on criterion c (+0.52 [0.38, 0.68], orange) and sensitivity d' (-0.003 [-0.33, 0.29], grey); the criterion shift is concentrated in OR-Bench-hard items.">
        <img src="figures/fig_sdt_v0.png" alt="Bar chart showing false-alarm rates for Gemma and GaMS3 in English and Slovene, and a forest plot of difference-in-differences for criterion c and sensitivity d-prime">
      </button>
      <figcaption>
        <strong>Criterion shift across models and languages.</strong>
        Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe items).
        (a) False-alarm rate F: Gemma rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene); GaMS3 stays at 0.273.
        (b) DiD<sub>c</sub> = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]; DiD<sub>d'</sub> = -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29].
      </figcaption>
    </figure>
  </div>

  <div class="table-wrap">
    <table>
      <caption class="sr-only">Signal-detection parameters by model and language</caption>
      <thead>
        <tr><th></th><th>Gemma EN</th><th>Gemma SL</th><th>GaMS3 EN</th><th>GaMS3 SL</th></tr>
      </thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><td>Hit rate (H)</td><td>0.89</td><td>0.94</td><td>0.90</td><td>0.86</td></tr>
        <tr><td>False-alarm rate (F)</td><td>0.364</td><td>0.569</td><td>0.273</td><td>0.273</td></tr>
        <tr><td>d'</td><td>1.57</td><td>1.39</td><td>1.86</td><td>1.68</td></tr>
        <tr><td>c</td><td>-0.44</td><td>-0.87</td><td>-0.33</td><td>-0.23</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
  </div>
  <p class="code-link">
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-2/experiment-5" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Code: Slovene vs English refusal: GaMS3 vs Gemma-3 confirmation</a>
  </p>

  <h3>Reply-language refusal (estimate)</h3>
  <p>
    In the 3 x 3 crossed grid (Experiment 14), edited Gemma at high dose shows higher residual
    refusal when replying in Slovene than in English, regardless of prompt language. The raw
    mechanism contrast is OUT<sub>SL</sub> = +1.14 [0.60, 1.56] log-odds for Gemma; for GaMS3 the
    output-language contrast is -0.44 [-0.98, 0.27], spanning zero.
  </p>
  <p>
    This finding is rated ESTIMATE. The PPI-corrected output-language contrast for Gemma is
    0.20 [-0.76, 1.13], consistent with zero. The pre-registered four-readout robustness gate
    yields robust = False. The adjudicator agrees with the primary judge at kappa = 0.12 in the
    Gemma Slovene-edited cell (Se = 0.927, Sp = 0.714, n = 48).
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 16</a>
    provides a confirmatory point estimate (OUT<sub>Gemma</sub> = +2.43 [+0.89, +5.38] on a held-out 294-item set),
    but the judge-specificity concern persists.
  </p>
  <div class="figure-container">
    <figure>
      <button class="fig-trigger" data-fig="figures/fig_grid_v0.png" data-caption="Refusal rates on harmful items in the crossed prompt-language x reply-language design (Experiment 14, 200 harmful items per cell), at each model's high edit dose: (a) Gemma (lambda = 1.0) and (b) GaMS3 (lambda = 0.625). Gemma refuses 0.56-0.83 in the Slovene-reply column against 0.07-0.18 in the English-reply column. GaMS3 stays at 0.12-0.28 in every cell. Hatched cells have under 90% language compliance.">
        <img src="figures/fig_grid_v0.png" alt="Two 3-by-3 heatmaps showing refusal rates by prompt and reply language for Gemma and GaMS3, with Gemma showing high refusal in Slovene-output cells and GaMS3 showing uniform low refusal">
      </button>
      <figcaption>
        <strong>Crossed prompt-language x reply-language refusal grid.</strong>
        (a) Gemma at lambda = 1.0: Slovene-reply column 0.56-0.83, English-reply column 0.07-0.18.
        (b) GaMS3 at lambda = 0.625: uniform 0.12-0.28. Hatched cells: under 90% language compliance.
      </figcaption>
    </figure>
  </div>

  <h3>Dose-response</h3>
  <p>
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-3/experiment-9" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Experiment 9</a>
    measures refusal rates across nine lambda values (300 items per condition). Gemma's Slovene
    dose-response curve is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more
    Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3 shows a smaller, non-significant shift. The cross-model
    difference at matched 50% English refusal is G<sub>3</sub> = -0.97 [-1.56, -0.44] log-odds
    (verdict: ESTIMATE; model-label permutation p = 0.084). The
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-15" target="_blank" rel="noopener">13-step dense dose ladder (Experiment 15)</a>
    confirms the gap is present across the full dose range.
  </p>

  <h3>Cross-model specificity</h3>
  <p>
    The cross-model output-language specificity contrast is dOUT<sub>SL</sub> = -1.58 [-2.22, -0.66]
    (MDE 1.07): Gemma's output-language effect is larger than GaMS3's.
    The input-language specificity contrast is dIN<sub>SL</sub> = -0.26 [-1.13, 0.57] (MDE 1.19):
    the two models do not measurably differ in input-language sensitivity.
  </p>

  <h3>Compliant-row contrast</h3>
  <p>
    Restricting to rows where both models achieve over 90% language compliance (English-input rows only),
    the edit-induced refusal lag in the EN-to-SL cell is -1.26 [-2.17, 0.20], which includes zero.
  </p>

  <h3>Inconclusive and null results</h3>
  <p>
    The unedited GaMS3 shows a refusal gap of -1.17 [-2.83, 0.22] relative to Gemma in the
    SL-to-SL cell: inconclusive, with a fragility index of 1 and near-ceiling refusal rates.
    All Hungarian contrasts are uninformative (MDE approximately 3 log-odds units). The
    <a href="https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-17" target="_blank" rel="noopener">RefusEU validation (Experiment 17)</a>
    on 1,300 items per language is inconclusive (MDE over 2), consistent with near-ceiling refusal rates.
  </p>
</section>

<!-- LIMITATIONS -->
<section id="limitations">
  <h2>Limitations</h2>
  <ul class="limitations-list">
    <li><strong>Sample size.</strong> The adjudication sample is 30 items per cell, limiting the precision of judge-validity estimates. The false-alarm rate estimates rest on 1,093 safe items, adequate for the pooled contrast but noisy at the per-category level.</li>
    <li><strong>Judge specificity.</strong> The primary judge achieves Sp = 0.714 in the Gemma Slovene-edited cell, meaning roughly 29% of non-refusals are misclassified as refusals. This inflates the raw refusal rate and weakens the reply-language finding. PPI correction depends on the gold-label quality of the Sonnet 4.5 adjudicator, itself an LLM.</li>
    <li><strong>Language compliance.</strong> Four cells (SL-to-EN, HU-to-EN, SL-to-HU, HU-to-SL) fall below 90% compliance, limiting the crossed-grid analysis to compliant rows for mechanism claims.</li>
    <li><strong>Quantization.</strong> Both models run in NF4 quantization. The interaction between quantization and directional ablation is not characterized.</li>
    <li><strong>Novelty.</strong> Over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by prior work. The contribution is the signal-detection decomposition (criterion vs. sensitivity) and the controlled abliteration design, not the observation itself.</li>
  </ul>
</section>

target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\" class=\"secondary\">Code repository</a>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"round-links\">\n    Round reports:\n    <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-1/report.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Round 1</a> ·\n    <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-2/report.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Round 2</a> ·\n    <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-3/report.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Round 3</a> ·\n    <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/report.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Round 4</a> ·\n    <a href=\"https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive@fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/report.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Round 5</a>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<!-- CONTRIBUTIONS -->\n<section id=\"contributions\">\n  <h2>Contributions</h2>\n  <div class=\"contrib-grid\">\n    <div class=\"contrib-card\">\n      <span class=\"card-label\">Primary finding</span>\n      <h3>Over-refusal as criterion shift</h3>\n      <p>\n        Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at nearly twice the English rate. Signal-detection\n        analysis attributes this to a criterion shift (DiD<sub>c</sub> = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68])\n        with no corresponding change in sensitivity (DiD<sub>d'</sub> = -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29]),\n        replicated across four experiments.\n      </p>\n    </div>\n    <div class=\"contrib-card\">\n      <span class=\"card-label\">Secondary analysis</span>\n      <h3>Reply-language refusal (estimate)</h3>\n      <p>\n        A crossed 3 x 3 design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma\n        (OUT<sub>SL</sub> = +1.14 [0.60, 1.56] log-odds), but prediction-powered inference\n        correction is consistent with zero (0.20 [-0.76, 1.13]) and the adjudicator agrees with the\n        primary judge at only kappa = 0.12 in Slovene.\n      </p>\n    </div>\n    <div class=\"contrib-card\">\n      <span class=\"card-label\">Methodology</span>\n      <h3>Measurement methodology for multilingual refusal</h3>\n      <p>\n        The study quantifies how judge specificity, language compliance, and correction methods\n        interact when evaluating multilingual refusal, showing that low specificity on edited\n        Slovene text inflates raw refusal estimates.\n      </p>\n    </div>\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<!-- METHOD -->\n<section id=\"method\">\n  <h2>Method</h2>\n  <p>\n    The study compares two 12-billion-parameter models built on the same base:\n    <strong>Gemma-3-12B-IT</strong> and <strong>GaMS3-12B-Instruct</strong>, a Slovene-adapted\n    variant with continued pretraining and DPO alignment. Both run in NF4 quantization.\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Abliteration edit</h3>\n  <p>\n    The de-censoring intervention uses directional ablation of the refusal direction in the residual\n    stream, applied via per-layer LoRA adapters optimized by a 40-trial tree-structured Parzen\n    estimation (TPE) search. Each trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from\n    contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts, and projects it out. Two edit doses\n    bracket the 50% English refusal point: a low dose (lambda = 0.5 for both models) and a high\n    dose (lambda = 1.0 for Gemma, 0.625 for GaMS3).\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Over-refusal measurement (signal detection)</h3>\n  <p>\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-2/experiment-5\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 5</a>\n    tests 1,093 safe items (XSTest + OR-Bench) and 349 harmful items in English and Slovene.\n    A Qwen3-14B judge classifies each response as refused or complied. Hit rate (refusal on harmful)\n    and false-alarm rate (refusal on safe) yield signal-detection parameters d' (sensitivity) and\n    c (criterion). The key contrast: DiD<sub>c</sub> = (GaMS3<sub>SL</sub> - GaMS3<sub>EN</sub>)\n    - (Gemma<sub>SL</sub> - Gemma<sub>EN</sub>).\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Crossed grid (reply-language refusal)</h3>\n  <p>\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-14\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 14</a>\n    crosses three prompt languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) with three reply languages in a\n    3 x 3 grid. Each cell contains 200 harmful items at three dose levels (zero, low, high).\n    The output-language contrast OUT<sub>SL</sub> measures the mean log-odds refusal gap between\n    Slovene-output and English-output cells, averaged over prompt languages.\n    Cells where fewer than 90% of model replies match the requested language are flagged.\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Judges and corrections</h3>\n  <p>\n    Judge accuracy is assessed against a Sonnet 4.5 adjudicator on 30 items per cell.\n    Prediction-powered inference (PPI++) corrects the raw estimates against this gold standard.\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 16</a>\n    uses a held-out set of 294 items as a PPI confirmation.\n  </p>\n</section>\n\n<!-- RESULTS -->\n<section id=\"results\">\n  <h2>Results</h2>\n\n  <h3>Over-refusal: criterion shift on benign items</h3>\n  <div class=\"stat-row\">\n    <div class=\"stat-box\">\n      <div class=\"stat-value\">0.569</div>\n      <div class=\"stat-label\">Gemma SL false-alarm rate</div>\n    </div>\n    <div class=\"stat-box\">\n      <div class=\"stat-value\">0.364</div>\n      <div class=\"stat-label\">Gemma EN false-alarm rate</div>\n    </div>\n    <div class=\"stat-box\">\n      <div class=\"stat-value\">0.273</div>\n      <div class=\"stat-label\">GaMS3 (both languages)</div>\n    </div>\n  </div>\n  <p>\n    Gemma applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than in English on benign items.\n    GaMS3 does not. The DiD on criterion c is +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]: Gemma's Slovene criterion\n    shifts by half a standard deviation relative to GaMS3. The DiD on d' is -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29],\n    indistinguishable from zero. The asymmetry is entirely in the threshold.\n  </p>\n  <p>\n    The criterion shift replicates across three further experiments.\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-14\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 14</a>\n    yields DiD<sub>c</sub> = -1.56 [-1.97, -1.29] (Gemma minus GaMS3, high dose, SL-output cells).\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 16</a>\n    confirms on a held-out set.\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/evaluation-4\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Evaluation 4</a>\n    re-judges the same items with an independent adjudicator, yielding DiD<sub>c</sub> in [0.39, 0.67].\n  </p>\n  <div class=\"figure-container\">\n    <figure>\n      <button class=\"fig-trigger\" data-fig=\"figures/fig_sdt_v0.png\" data-caption=\"Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe XSTest/OR-Bench items; refusal labels from the Qwen3-14B judge). (a) False-alarm rate F for Gemma and GaMS3 in English (blue) and Slovene (orange); Gemma's false-alarm rate rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene), while GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both languages. (b) Difference-in-differences on criterion c (+0.52 [0.38, 0.68], orange) and sensitivity d' (-0.003 [-0.33, 0.29], grey); the criterion shift is concentrated in OR-Bench-hard items.\">\n        <img src=\"figures/fig_sdt_v0.png\" alt=\"Bar chart showing false-alarm rates for Gemma and GaMS3 in English and Slovene, and a forest plot of difference-in-differences for criterion c and sensitivity d-prime\">\n      </button>\n      <figcaption>\n        <strong>Criterion shift across models and languages.</strong>\n        Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe items).\n        (a) False-alarm rate F: Gemma rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene); GaMS3 stays at 0.273.\n        (b) DiD<sub>c</sub> = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]; DiD<sub>d'</sub> = -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29].\n      </figcaption>\n    </figure>\n  </div>\n\n  <div class=\"table-wrap\">\n    <table>\n      <caption class=\"sr-only\">Signal-detection parameters by model and language</caption>\n      <thead>\n        <tr><th></th><th>Gemma EN</th><th>Gemma SL</th><th>GaMS3 EN</th><th>GaMS3 SL</th></tr>\n      </thead>\n      <tbody>\n        <tr><td>Hit rate (H)</td><td>0.89</td><td>0.94</td><td>0.90</td><td>0.86</td></tr>\n        <tr><td>False-alarm rate (F)</td><td>0.364</td><td>0.569</td><td>0.273</td><td>0.273</td></tr>\n        <tr><td>d'</td><td>1.57</td><td>1.39</td><td>1.86</td><td>1.68</td></tr>\n        <tr><td>c</td><td>-0.44</td><td>-0.87</td><td>-0.33</td><td>-0.23</td></tr>\n      </tbody>\n    </table>\n  </div>\n  <p class=\"code-link\">\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-2/experiment-5\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Code: Slovene vs English refusal: GaMS3 vs Gemma-3 confirmation</a>\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Reply-language refusal (estimate)</h3>\n  <p>\n    In the 3 x 3 crossed grid (Experiment 14), edited Gemma at high dose shows higher residual\n    refusal when replying in Slovene than in English, regardless of prompt language. The raw\n    mechanism contrast is OUT<sub>SL</sub> = +1.14 [0.60, 1.56] log-odds for Gemma; for GaMS3 the\n    output-language contrast is -0.44 [-0.98, 0.27], spanning zero.\n  </p>\n  <p>\n    This finding is rated ESTIMATE. The PPI-corrected output-language contrast for Gemma is\n    0.20 [-0.76, 1.13], consistent with zero. The pre-registered four-readout robustness gate\n    yields robust = False. The adjudicator agrees with the primary judge at kappa = 0.12 in the\n    Gemma Slovene-edited cell (Se = 0.927, Sp = 0.714, n = 48).\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-16\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 16</a>\n    provides a confirmatory point estimate (OUT<sub>Gemma</sub> = +2.43 [+0.89, +5.38] on a held-out 294-item set),\n    but the judge-specificity concern persists.\n  </p>\n  <div class=\"figure-container\">\n    <figure>\n      <button class=\"fig-trigger\" data-fig=\"figures/fig_grid_v0.png\" data-caption=\"Refusal rates on harmful items in the crossed prompt-language x reply-language design (Experiment 14, 200 harmful items per cell), at each model's high edit dose: (a) Gemma (lambda = 1.0) and (b) GaMS3 (lambda = 0.625). Gemma refuses 0.56-0.83 in the Slovene-reply column against 0.07-0.18 in the English-reply column. GaMS3 stays at 0.12-0.28 in every cell. Hatched cells have under 90% language compliance.\">\n        <img src=\"figures/fig_grid_v0.png\" alt=\"Two 3-by-3 heatmaps showing refusal rates by prompt and reply language for Gemma and GaMS3, with Gemma showing high refusal in Slovene-output cells and GaMS3 showing uniform low refusal\">\n      </button>\n      <figcaption>\n        <strong>Crossed prompt-language x reply-language refusal grid.</strong>\n        (a) Gemma at lambda = 1.0: Slovene-reply column 0.56-0.83, English-reply column 0.07-0.18.\n        (b) GaMS3 at lambda = 0.625: uniform 0.12-0.28. Hatched cells: under 90% language compliance.\n      </figcaption>\n    </figure>\n  </div>\n\n  <h3>Dose-response</h3>\n  <p>\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-3/experiment-9\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">Experiment 9</a>\n    measures refusal rates across nine lambda values (300 items per condition). Gemma's Slovene\n    dose-response curve is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more\n    Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3 shows a smaller, non-significant shift. The cross-model\n    difference at matched 50% English refusal is G<sub>3</sub> = -0.97 [-1.56, -0.44] log-odds\n    (verdict: ESTIMATE; model-label permutation p = 0.084). The\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-4/experiment-15\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">13-step dense dose ladder (Experiment 15)</a>\n    confirms the gap is present across the full dose range.\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Cross-model specificity</h3>\n  <p>\n    The cross-model output-language specificity contrast is dOUT<sub>SL</sub> = -1.58 [-2.22, -0.66]\n    (MDE 1.07): Gemma's output-language effect is larger than GaMS3's.\n    The input-language specificity contrast is dIN<sub>SL</sub> = -0.26 [-1.13, 0.57] (MDE 1.19):\n    the two models do not measurably differ in input-language sensitivity.\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Compliant-row contrast</h3>\n  <p>\n    Restricting to rows where both models achieve over 90% language compliance (English-input rows only),\n    the edit-induced refusal lag in the EN-to-SL cell is -1.26 [-2.17, 0.20], which includes zero.\n  </p>\n\n  <h3>Inconclusive and null results</h3>\n  <p>\n    The unedited GaMS3 shows a refusal gap of -1.17 [-2.83, 0.22] relative to Gemma in the\n    SL-to-SL cell: inconclusive, with a fragility index of 1 and near-ceiling refusal rates.\n    All Hungarian contrasts are uninformative (MDE approximately 3 log-odds units). The\n    <a href=\"https://github.com/ai-inventor-papers/ai-invention-2cf2a7-does-slovene-taught-refusal-survive/tree/fork/run_2MI56L8wzgdI/round-5/experiment-17\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"noopener\">RefusEU validation (Experiment 17)</a>\n    on 1,300 items per language is inconclusive (MDE over 2), consistent with near-ceiling refusal rates.\n  </p>\n</section>\n\n<!-- FIGURE GALLERY -->\n<section id=\"figures\">\n  <h2>Figures</h2>\n  <div class=\"gallery-grid\">\n\n    <div class=\"figure-container\">\n      <figure>\n        <button class=\"fig-trigger\" data-fig=\"figures/fig_sdt_v0.png\" data-caption=\"Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe XSTest/OR-Bench items; refusal labels from the Qwen3-14B judge; English = back-translation, Slovene = machine translation of the same items). (a) False-alarm rate F, the proportion of the 1,093 safe items refused, for Gemma and GaMS3 in English (blue) and Slovene (orange); error bars are Wilson 95% CIs and the dashed grey line marks F = 0.5. Gemma's false-alarm rate rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene), while GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both languages. (b) Difference-in-differences on the criterion c (DiD_c, orange-red) and on sensitivity d' (DiD_d', grey), in z units, with 95% percentile CIs from 2,000 item-level bootstrap resamples; the dashed line marks zero. The criterion shift is +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]; the sensitivity shift, -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29], is indistinguishable from zero.\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_sdt_v0.png\" alt=\"Bar chart of false-alarm rates showing Gemma's Slovene rate at 0.569 versus 0.364 in English, with GaMS3 at 0.273 in both; forest plot of DiD on criterion and sensitivity\">\n        </button>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Criterion Shift Across Models and Languages.</strong>\n          Signal-detection parameters on the HARD set from Experiment 5 (349 harmful and 1,093 safe XSTest/OR-Bench items; refusal labels from the Qwen3-14B judge; English = back-translation, Slovene = machine translation of the same items). (a) False-alarm rate F for Gemma and GaMS3 in English (blue) and Slovene (orange); error bars are Wilson 95% CIs. Gemma's false-alarm rate rises from 0.364 (English) to 0.569 (Slovene), while GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both languages. (b) Difference-in-differences on the criterion c (+0.52 [0.38, 0.68], orange-red) and on sensitivity d' (-0.003 [-0.33, 0.29], grey), with 95% percentile CIs from 2,000 item-level bootstrap resamples. The criterion shift is concentrated in OR-Bench-hard items and reverses sign when partial answers are coded as refusals.\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n    </div>\n\n    <div class=\"figure-container\">\n      <figure>\n        <button class=\"fig-trigger\" data-fig=\"figures/fig_grid_v0.png\" data-caption=\"Refusal rates on harmful items in the crossed prompt-language x requested-reply-language design (Experiment 14, 200 harmful items per cell), at each model's high edit dose: (a) Gemma (lambda = 1.0) and (b) GaMS3 (lambda = 0.625). Rows give the prompt language and columns the requested reply language. Colour encodes the refusal rate on a shared 0-1 scale (blue below 0.5, red above), and each cell shows the rate with its Wilson 95% CI in brackets. Hatched cells are those where under 90% of replies were written in the requested language. All four are GaMS3 cells (SL-to-EN, SL-to-HU, HU-to-EN, HU-to-SL), so off the English-input row they do not measure the requested reply language. Gemma refuses 0.56-0.83 in the Slovene-reply column for every prompt language, against 0.07-0.18 in the English-reply column. GaMS3 stays at 0.12-0.28 in every cell. Refusal is scored by the primary judge, and the two panels use different edit strengths.\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_grid_v0.png\" alt=\"Two 3-by-3 heatmaps of refusal rates by prompt and reply language showing Gemma's strong Slovene-output reserve versus GaMS3's uniform rates\">\n        </button>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Crossed Prompt-Language x Reply-Language Refusal Grid.</strong>\n          Refusal rates on harmful items in the crossed design (Experiment 14, 200 harmful items per cell), at each model's high edit dose: (a) Gemma (lambda = 1.0) and (b) GaMS3 (lambda = 0.625). Rows give the prompt language and columns the requested reply language. Colour encodes the refusal rate on a shared 0-1 scale. Hatched cells have under 90% language compliance. Gemma refuses 0.56-0.83 in the Slovene-reply column against 0.07-0.18 in the English-reply column. GaMS3 stays at 0.12-0.28 in every cell.\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n    </div>\n\n    <div class=\"figure-container\">\n      <figure>\n        <button class=\"fig-trigger\" data-fig=\"figures/fig_dose_v0.png\" data-caption=\"Refusal rate on harmful prompts as a function of abliteration dose lambda (Experiment 9). Lambda scales each model's own selected English-objective edit (lambda = 0: unedited model; lambda = 1: the selected edit), so the comparison that holds is English vs. Slovene within a model. Blue: Gemma-3-12B-IT; green: GaMS3-12B-Instruct. Solid lines with filled markers: English probes; dashed lines with open markers: Slovene probes. Points are raw refusal proportions from the distilled J1 judge. Shaded bands are Wilson 95% intervals. n = 300 items per model and language at lambda = 0 and n = 100 at each of the 8 edited steps. Gemma's Slovene curve lies above its English curve at every dose, with a 0.21-0.32 gap between lambda = 0.5 and 1. GaMS3's gap is smaller (at most 0.14) and closes by lambda = 1.\">\n          <img src=\"figures/fig_dose_v0.png\" alt=\"Line chart of refusal rate versus abliteration dose for Gemma and GaMS3 in English and Slovene, showing Gemma's Slovene curve above its English curve at every dose\">\n        </button>\n        <figcaption>\n          <strong>Dose-Response Curves for Refusal Under Abliteration.</strong>\n          Refusal rate on harmful prompts as a function of abliteration dose lambda (Experiment 9). Lambda scales each model's own English-objective edit (0 = unedited; 1 = selected edit). Blue: Gemma; green: GaMS3. Solid/filled: English; dashed/open: Slovene. n = 300 items at lambda = 0, n = 100 at each edited step. Gemma's Slovene curve lies above its English curve at every dose, with a 0.21-0.32 gap between lambda = 0.5 and 1. GaMS3's gap is smaller (at most 0.14) and closes by lambda = 1. The cross-model difference at matched 50% English refusal (G<sub>3</sub> = -0.97 [-1.56, -0.44] log-odds) did not meet pre-registered confirmation criteria (verdict: ESTIMATE; permutation p = 0.084).\n        </figcaption>\n      </figure>\n    </div>\n\n  </div>\n</section>\n\n<!-- LIMITATIONS -->\n<section id=\"limitations\">\n  <h2>Limitations</h2>\n  <ul class=\"limitations-list\">\n    <li><strong>Sample size.</strong> The adjudication sample is 30 items per cell, limiting the precision of judge-validity estimates. The false-alarm rate estimates rest on 1,093 safe items, adequate for the pooled contrast but noisy at the per-category level.</li>\n    <li><strong>Judge specificity.</strong> The primary judge achieves Sp = 0.714 in the Gemma Slovene-edited cell, meaning roughly 29% of non-refusals are misclassified as refusals. This inflates the raw refusal rate and weakens the reply-language finding. PPI correction depends on the gold-label quality of the Sonnet 4.5 adjudicator, itself an LLM.</li>\n    <li><strong>Language compliance.</strong> Four cells (SL-to-EN, HU-to-EN, SL-to-HU, HU-to-SL) fall below 90% compliance, limiting the crossed-grid analysis to compliant rows for mechanism claims.</li>\n    <li><strong>Quantization.</strong> Both models run in NF4 quantization. The interaction between quantization and directional ablation is not characterized.</li>\n    <li><strong>Novelty.</strong> Over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by prior work. The contribution is the signal-detection decomposition (criterion vs. sensitivity) and the controlled abliteration design, not the observation itself.</li>\n  </ul>\n</section>\n\n<!-- FOOTER
